edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle · Week 7 · Grades K–1 (header); bare page number "1" as the only footer
edits.fix: Header: "Week 7 / Take-away games / Grades K–1". Footer: "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>" on every page.

edits.quote: It is your turn. Can you take the last counter on this turn? Circle yes or no under each pile.
edits.fix: Delete. With piles of 1, 2 and 3 it only restates the rules, which the whole-group demonstration already covers. Renumber the remaining problems.

edits.quote: There are 3 counters, and it is your turn. Your partner always plays carefully. Can you be the player who takes the last counter? Circle yes or no.
edits.fix: This one-pile yes/no is a small directed step toward P3, and pile 3 is already on the P3 chart. Fold it into P3, or widen it into a play problem: play from 3, 4 and 5 counters and circle whether you would rather go first or second.

edits.quote: A pile is a trap when the player whose turn it is will lose if the other player plays carefully. (separate boxed definition placed above P3 on page 2)
edits.fix: Move the trap definition into the opening rules box on page 1, so the activity-wide rules are stated once at the start. It is used again in P7 and P8.

edits.quote: You will play against the adult at your table with a pile of 9 counters.
edits.fix: 9 is already marked on the P3 chart, so the circled choice is just looked up. Use a pile beyond the chart, e.g. 14, so the child has to extend the pattern before playing the adult.

k-1.summary: A solid K–1 set: real backward induction on piles 1–12 with drawn counters, a strategy that answers both replies (P4), finding the mistake in a recorded game (P5), extending the pattern past 20, a rule change to {1,2,3}, and simple two-pile games. All answers check out (traps 3, 6, 9, 12; then 4, 8, 12; P5 row 3; P9 second, first, second, second, first). The edits are a trivial opening (P1, P2), a misplaced definition box, a look-up in P6, and the Name field and header/footer template.

edits.quote: Name ____________ (Name field at the right of the header on every page)
edits.fix: Delete the Name field from the page template.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle · Week 7 · Grades 2–3 (header); bare page number "1" as the only footer
edits.fix: Header: "Week 7 / Take-away games / Grades 2–3". Footer: "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>" on every page.

edits.quote: A player claims: “If the pile has at least 4 counters and you can win, then taking 4 counters is a way to win.” Is the claim correct?
edits.fix: Once P2 is done, pile 5 refutes this in seconds, and "Is the claim correct?" invites a bare "no". Make it a real search: "For which winning piles up to 20 is taking 4 a way to win?" (answer: 4, 6, 11, 13, 18, 20).

edits.quote: Is the claim correct?
edits.fix: Say what to record: "If not, show a game from 8 where copying loses." Otherwise children stop at yes or no without testing the claim against each first move (it fails after the first player takes 1).

grades-2-3.summary: The strongest band. It classifies piles under {1, 3, 4}, tests two claimed strategies, finds the mistakes in a recorded game (turns 2 and 3), builds a plan from 14 against every reply, extends the period-7 pattern to 100, contrasts it with the parity pattern of {1, 3, 5}, and plays two-pile sums including the non-mirror case 6 and 4. Every answer checks out. The only edits are a P3 that is too quick, an unclear stopping point in P4, and the template fixes.

edits.quote: Name ____________ (Name field at the right of the header on every page)
edits.fix: Delete the Name field from the page template.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle · Week 7 · Grades 4–5 (header); bare page number "1" as the only footer
edits.fix: Header: "Week 7 / Take-away games / Grades 4–5". Footer: "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>" on every page.

edits.quote: Allowed moves {1, 2}. Describe all the losing piles, and explain why your description is correct for piles of every size.
edits.fix: The band opens with a proof, and no page asks children to play with counters. Start P1 with play on a named pile (e.g. 10) and a 0–15 strip to record L/W, then ask for the description and the reason.

edits.quote: This player moves first, and the opponent plays carefully.
edits.fix: Write "the opponent knows this habit and plays to win". At a losing pile (e.g. 9, after the greedy player takes 4 from 13) a 'careful' opponent has no standard winning move, so children may answer "piles 4 or 6 more than a losing pile". The real answer is only 1, 3, 4, 6 and 11.

edits.quote: Find every set of allowed moves that contains 1 and has exactly the same losing piles as {1, 3, 5}.
edits.fix: Delete "that contains 1". Pile 1 must be a winning pile, so working out that 1 is needed is part of the problem (answer: exactly the sets of odd numbers containing 1).

edits.quote: Allowed moves {1, 2, m}, where m is a whole number larger than 2. For which m are the losing piles exactly the multiples of 3, as they are for {1, 2}? For every other m, describe the losing piles.
edits.fix: Drop the variable notation for fourth graders: "Add a third allowed move to {1, 2}. Which third moves keep the losing piles exactly the multiples of 3? For the others, describe the losing piles." (Answer: non-multiples of 3 keep them; for a multiple of 3, m, the losing piles leave remainder 0, 3, ..., m−3 on division by m+1.)

edits.quote: Explain why, for every finite set of allowed moves, the labels W and L eventually repeat in a cycle forever.
edits.fix: A general pigeonhole proof over every finite set is too abstract to start from for grades 4–5. Ask it for a specific set first (e.g. {1, 6, 9} from P6, where each label depends on the 9 before it), with the general statement for the adult to pursue.

edits.quote: In a game with two piles, a player chooses one pile on each turn and removes an allowed number of counters from that pile only. Whoever takes the last counter wins. Give each single pile a value. ... (second boxed rules block mid-page 4)
edits.fix: Shared rules belong once at the start. Put the value definition in P8, which uses only single piles, and the two-pile rule in P9, where it is first needed.

edits.quote: Allowed moves {1, 3, 4}. Find the value of each pile from 0 to 20.
edits.fix: Values are defined and tabulated before anyone plays a two-pile game, so the formal tool comes before the question it answers. Add a short two-pile play problem with small piles first (e.g. 2 and 2, 3 and 1, 4 and 2, 6 and 4), then introduce the values.

edits.quote: Explain why, with two piles, the player about to move loses against careful play when the two values are equal, and can win when the two values are different.
edits.fix: The rule P9 asks children to find is printed directly below P9, so P9 turns into a look-up. Reword: "Find a rule, using the two values, that tells whether the player about to move can win, and explain why it always works."

grades-4-5.summary: The mathematics is deep and correct: {1, 2} and {1, 3, 4} periodicity, greedy play (wins only from 1, 3, 4, 6 and 11), sets with the parity pattern, {1, 2, m}, a preperiod of 10 and cycle of 5 for {1, 6, 9}, Grundy values, and two-pile sums (6/4 and 12/5 lose; 5/1 and 11/3 win). But the band is abstract and proof-first, with no play and with set and variable notation. Values are handed over before any two-pile experience, and P10 gives away P9. There is far more than forty minutes of material.

overall.strongest: The grades 2–3 band is the strongest: a well-sequenced, correct, concrete set around {1, 3, 4} that tests claimed strategies against every reply and ends with two-pile sums.
overall.weakest: The grades 4–5 band is the weakest: it opens with proofs, never asks children to play, and introduces Grundy values formally before any two-pile play, so it needs about half an hour of edits.
